sentences.text: Phuwiangosaurus was a mid-sized titanosauriform dinosaur that lived in Thailand during the Early Cretaceous, reaching lengths between 15 and 20 meters.
Scientists estimate its mass to be approximately 17 tonnes.
Its teeth were slender and peg-like, with a height more than four times their base width.
The neck of this animal was likely composed of 13 vertebrae.
Numerous juvenile bones have been found, which is rare for sauropods.
Fossil evidence indicates that theropod dinosaurs fed on Phuwiangosaurus.
The species Phuwiangosaurus sirindhornae was formally named in 1994 by Martin, Buffetaut, and Suteethorn.
The species name honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, and the genus name refers to the Phu Wiang area where the fossils were found.
The type specimen was discovered in Phu Wiang National Park in 1982 and prepared over several years.
The holotype is a partial adult skeleton including vertebrae, ribs, shoulder bones, and leg bones.
The most complete skeleton found is a half-grown individual that is about 60% complete and includes a partial skull.
Recent phylogenetic analyses place Phuwiangosaurus within the family Euhelopodidae.
Some classifications place Phuwiangosaurus in the family Nemegtosauridae.
Fossils were found in a floodplain environment with a humid, subtropical climate deposited between 133.6 and 132.1 million years ago.
It lived at the beginning of the Cretaceous period, approximately 140 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
The time range for the genus is estimated from the Barremian to the Aptian, spanning from 125.77 to 113.2 million years ago.
Some analyses suggest Phuwiangosaurus may be paraphyletic at the base of Somphospondyli rather than belonging to Euhelopodidae.
